sections.title: Definition & Unique Anatomy
sections.content: The 4th cranial nerve (Trochlear) is the longest and thinnest cranial nerve, and the only one to exit the brainstem dorsally and decussate before exiting. It innervates the Superior Oblique (SO) muscle. Its unique course makes it highly susceptible to trauma, particularly at the point of decussation in the anterior medullary velum.

sections.title: Epidemiological Distribution of Acquired IV Nerve Palsy

rows: Early childhood, often subclinical until decompensation
Often absent due to suppression or large fusion
Present (hypoplasia on the side of tilt)

sections.title: The Park-Bielschowsky Three-Step Test
content: Step 1: Identify which eye is hypertropic in primary position (e.g., Right Hypertropia).
Step 2: Determine if the hypertropia is worse in Right or Left gaze (e.g., worse in Left gaze).
Step 3: Determine if the hypertropia is worse on Right or Left head tilt (e.g., worse on Right tilt).
Conclusion: If RHT is worse in L-gaze and R-tilt, it confirms a Right Superior Oblique (CN IV) palsy.

sections.title: Signs of Bilateral CN IV Palsy
content: Excyclotorsion > 10 degrees (measured by Double Maddox Rod)
Reversing Hypertropia (RHT on L-tilt, LHT on R-tilt)
V-pattern Esotropia > 15 PD difference between up/down gaze
Underaction of both Superior Obliques / Overaction of both Inferior Obliques
Small hypertropia in primary position despite large symptoms

content.explanation: Superiors are IN-torsionists. (Superior Oblique and Superior Rectus both intort the eye).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Ipsilateral Hypertropia (worsens in adduction)
Excyclotorsion (subjective and objective fundus torsion)
Abnormal Head Position: Tilt to the contralateral shoulder
V-pattern esotropia (due to loss of SO abducting effect in depression)
Pseudo-overaction of the Inferior Oblique

rows: Restrictive pattern, lid lag, positive forced ductions
Associated with brainstem signs, torsion follows tilt (donkey ear)
Restriction in elevation in adduction, positive traction test
Associated ptosis, pupil involvement, horizontal component

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Orthoptic Assessment (Prism Cover Test in 9 positions).
2. Double Maddox Rod (Measure subjective torsion).
3. FAT Test (Family Album Tomography) for congenital signs.
4. Forced Duction Test (Differentiate palsy from restriction).
5. Neuroimaging (MRI Brain/Orbit) if non-vasculopathic/traumatic or progression.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Observation: 6-12 months for acquired/ischemic cases (spontaneous recovery common).
Prisms: Base-down prism (ipsilateral) or Base-up (contralateral) for small deviations.
Botulinum Toxin: Injection into the IO to reduce overaction temporarily.
Surgery: Indicated for stable, large deviations or significant torticollis.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques
content: Inferior Oblique Weakening (Recession, Myectomy, Anteriorization): Primary choice for IO overaction.
Superior Oblique Tuck: Indicated for SO laxity/underaction, especially in congenital cases.
Harada-Ito Procedure: Splitting the SO tendon and anteriorizing the lateral half to treat excyclotorsion.
Contralateral Inferior Rectus Recession: Effective for limiting deviation in the primary and down-gaze fields.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (BCSC Level)
content: In bilateral cases, the hypertropia may be 'masked'. Always check torsion and V-pattern.
A large vertical fusion amplitude (>6 PD) is pathognomonic for a long-standing (congenital) palsy.
In traumatic cases, CN IV is often damaged because the nerve decussates at the thin anterior medullary velum.
The 'FAT Test' refers to looking at old photos for a head tilt to prove chronicity.
Excyclotorsion > 10-15 degrees is the strongest indicator of bilateral involvement.
